name: Bronchogen
maker: St Petersburg Institute of Bioregulation and Gerontology (V. Khavinson)

overview.headline: A four-amino-acid peptide named for the lungs. Tested in bronchial cells and rats; never in a controlled human trial.
overview.lede: Bronchogen is the Khavinson institute's tetrapeptide Ala-Glu-Asp-Leu, patented in the U.S. in 2009 for "restoring respiratory organs function". In Russia it is a dietary supplement, not a medicine. In Canada and the U.S. it is sold only by "research peptide" vendors.

rats in the two lung-injury experiments, published only in the patent
controlled human trials in any language
stats.src: PubMed, patents, institute publications and registries, Oct 2026

mechanism.intro: A short peptide said to enter lung cells and switch on genes that keep the airway lining renewing.

parts.name: The bioregulator idea
parts.text: The institute's 2016 computer model places Bronchogen on the DNA sequence "ctcc" with "strong" predicted binding. A docking calculation, not a measurement in tissue.

parts.name: What the cell study showed
parts.text: In a human embryonic bronchial cell line the peptide raised the division marker Ki67 1.5- to 3.4-fold, lowered the stress protein p53 by about a third and increased lung-development genes (FOXA2 up to 15-fold). Whether it reaches a human lung has never been measured.

more.title: More: two spellings of one sequence
paras: The patent and the 2016 table give Ala-Glu-Asp-Leu; the group's main cell paper (Lung, 2014) calls the same product ADEL, Ala-Asp-Glu-Leu, a different molecule. The inconsistency has never been explained.

results.headline: Cell cultures and rats from one institute; a Russian claim of use in lung disease with no numbers.
results.lede: The only peer-reviewed data are changes in a cell line. The animal work is in the inventors' patent; the human claim is one sentence in a review.

stats.lbl: rise in the division marker Ki67 in "old" bronchial cell cultures

items.t: Human bronchial cells (FLECH line) at three passage ages: Ki67 up 1.55- to 3.42-fold; p53 down 28–38%; lung-development and surfactant genes up. Three samples per group, one laboratory.

Patent, 2009: 120 rats with staphylococcal lung infection repaired faster; 120 rats given bleomycin had less fibrosis (phagocytic indices 75.6 and 78.6 versus 46.3 and 57.6). Toxicity tests in 60 mice, 60 rats and 100 guinea pigs: none reported. Never peer reviewed.
A 2020 institute review calls oral Bronchogen "effective" in bronchopulmonary conditions, with no patient numbers, design or outcomes and no underlying paper we could find.

more.title: More: why the cell results are not a forecast
paras: A cell line has no immune system or airway and cannot show whether the peptide survives the trip from a capsule or injection site. The paper also reports a fall in the enzyme NOS-3 that its own table does not show.

effects.headline: No human safety data. The only toxicity testing is in the inventors' patent.
effects.lede: Nobody has given Bronchogen to people in a controlled study. The patent reports no rodent toxicity; the institute states generally that its peptides have no side effects. Neither replaces trial data.

disc.title: Stopping because of side effects
disc.text: Not measurable: no trial has been run.

unique.title: What is actually known
unique.text: Nothing beyond the absence of data. The peptide makes bronchial cells divide more and switches off p53, a tumour-suppressor protein, a signal a trial would follow for years.

more.title: More: what a trial would monitor for
paras: Immune reactions to an injected peptide of uncertain purity, and long-term effects of a cell-growth signal in airway tissue.

more.title: More: the good side effects
paras: In cells: more division. In rats: faster recovery from infection and less fibrosis, per the patent. In people: nothing measured.

urgent.title: Symptoms a doctor should see promptly
items: Spreading redness, swelling or pus at an injection site, or fever and chills after an injection
Hives, swelling of the face or throat, trouble breathing
Yellowing of the skin or eyes, dark urine
urgent.note: No trial has defined this peptide's own danger signs; these relate to an unverified product.

levels.nopk: No one has measured Bronchogen in a person's blood; no half-life or absorption figure exists for it in any species. There is nothing to build a curve from.

stats.src: PubMed, patents, institute publications and registries, Oct 2026

explain.t: The simulator on other pages needs a measured half-life; none exists for Bronchogen.

explain.b: Why the oral claim is contested.
explain.t: Pharmacologists expect peptides this short to be digested by gut and blood enzymes; the institute says they are absorbed intact. Nothing in people settles it.

more.title: More: what this page cannot tell you
paras: What is in a product sold as Bronchogen, or what repeated use does: no independent analysis exists, and no study has followed anyone beyond a few weeks.

trials.headline: No registered trial anywhere. The human claim is a single sentence.
trials.lede: The institute's reviews say Bronchogen has been used in Russian lung patients; no paper with patient numbers, a control group or outcomes could be found.

more.title: More: how the existing studies were run
paras: A bronchial cell line was exposed to the peptide and compared with untreated cells; rats were treated after a lung injury and compared with untreated animals. The Russian supplement is not required to run trials.

running.title: No registered trials
items: No clinical trial of Bronchogen on ClinicalTrials.gov or any registry we could find (October 2026).
The 2020 review's bronchopulmonary claim cites no published study.

find.text: Search the registry for "Bronchogen" and its sequence "AEDL". We found no registered trial.

status.headline: Not approved anywhere. A dietary supplement in Russia, a "research chemical" everywhere else.

items.label: Canada
items.text: Never authorised by Health Canada as a medicine or natural health product (October 2026).

items.label: United States
items.text: Not FDA-approved; absent from FDA's 503A compounding category list of 14 May 2026.

items.label: Russia
items.text: Not a registered medicine. The Russian drug directory RLS lists Бронхоген as a food supplement (БАД) from Firma-Vita, description approved October 2012. Supplements are registered on safety paperwork, not proof of effect.

cards.title: What a "bioregulator" claim rests on
cards.text: The claim is that a peptide copied from an organ extract reaches that organ and switches on its genes. For Bronchogen the support is:
items: Computer docking models, test-tube DNA work and cell cultures from one institute; no study has tracked one of these peptides into a human organ.

cards.title: What "research use only" means
cards.text: A "research use only" label is a legal device, not a safety rating. No regulator in Canada or the U.S. has checked what is in a vial sold as Bronchogen, and no toxicology or purity data have been filed in the West.
items: In Russia the same name is a food supplement; that says nothing about what is in a vial sold abroad under it.

cards.title: Symptoms to take to a doctor
cards.text: If any of these appear after using such a product, see a doctor and bring the product:
items: Fever, chills, or a hot, swollen injection site
Hives, swelling of the face or throat, trouble breathing
Yellowing of the skin or eyes, dark urine
cards.note: Report a reaction to MedEffect Canada (canada.ca/medeffect) or, in the U.S., FDA MedWatch (fda.gov/medwatch).

more.title: More: the Khavinson peptide family
paras: Vladimir Khavinson (1946–2024) directed the St Petersburg Institute of Bioregulation and Gerontology, which made animal-organ extracts from the 1970s and then designed two- to four-amino-acid peptides from each extract's amino-acid make-up, naming them after target organs. Six products became licensed medicines in the USSR or Russia: Thymalin (1982), Thymogen and Epithalamin (1990), Prostatilen (1992), Cortexin and Retinalamin (1999). The synthetic organ-named peptides sold online are not among them, and none appears in an international trial registry.
